title: AdPO: Adversarial Defense via Preference Optimization
one_liner: A vision-language model learns to prefer normal outputs on real images and reject misleading outputs on attacked images by teaching just the image encoder to compare clean and adversarial examples.
lead: Vision-language models like GPT-4o can understand both images and text, but they fail dangerously when images are subtly attacked with tiny pixel noise. Traditional adversarial training (brute-force exposure to attacks) damages clean performance. AdPO takes a different approach: it frames defense against attacks as a preference problem. The model learns to prefer normal outputs when it sees real images, and reject confused outputs when it sees attacked images — and it does all this by tuning just one part, the image encoder.

problem.h2: Vision-language models break under pixel attacks
paras: Vision-language models combine an image encoder (a neural network trained to extract visual features from photos) with a language model (which produces text). They work well on real images, but they are vulnerable: if you add imperceptibly small noise to an image, the model hallucinates or misunderstands it completely.

The obvious fix is adversarial training: show the model attacked images during training so it learns to handle them. But this backfires. When you expose the model to adversarial examples, it learns to be defensive in a general way — and that defensiveness damages its performance on clean, unattacked images. The model becomes pessimistic; it second-guesses itself on good inputs too.
The real problem is that adversarial training treats defense against attacks and clean accuracy as two separate, competing goals. The model cannot pursue both at once.

callout.html: Teach the image encoder to compare pairs: prefer the normal output when it sees a real image, reject the confused output when it sees an attacked image.

paras: The paper modifies only the image encoder (the visual feature extractor at the start of the model), leaving the language model frozen. This is key: by constraining the change to one part, the method is cheap to train and does not accidentally damage the language component that works well on clean inputs.
object.object: Image encoder weights (the numbers inside the visual feature extractor)

hidden.name: Preference margin on the pair
paras: Preference margin is the gap between how confident the model is in the correct answer and how confident it is in the wrong answer. When the margin is large, the model clearly prefers the right output, because a wide gap means the encoder strongly distinguishes the correct visual features from the wrong ones. When the margin is small, it is confused, uncertain, because the encoder barely separates them.

The paper measures this margin by comparing two log probabilities: the likelihood the encoder assigns to correct features from a clean image versus the likelihood it assigns to wrong features from an adversarial image. The bigger the gap, the stronger the preference, because a large difference means the encoder puts much more belief in the correct answer than the wrong one, and during training the model learns to expand this gap by pushing correct outputs higher and wrong outputs lower.

heat.caption: Darker cells show stronger preference margins after training. Top row: margin grows from small (confused) to large (confident).

reads.html: The model gets better at saying yes to correct images and no to attacked images because the preference margin (the gap between them) gets wider.

DPO training increases the log probability of the correct output on clean input, minus the log probability of the wrong output on adversarial input. This is preference optimization: raise what we like, lower what we dislike.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the alignment of two goals
paras: Preference optimization (also called Direct Preference Optimization, or DPO) is a training technique borrowed from language model alignment. The idea is simple: instead of asking the model to get right answers on all inputs (which leads to conflicting pressure because attacked images create contradictory signals), teach it to prefer one outcome over another — this avoids the conflict by replacing two separate goals with one clear ranking.

Here is the insight: defense against attacks and clean accuracy both need the model to produce correct outputs. The conflict only appears when you force the model to do both at once with equal weight. But if you reframe the problem as pairwise preference — prefer correct output on clean, prefer correct output on adversarial — you transform the two competing goals into a single coherent preference: choose the right answer, always. The language model learns to trust whichever visual features the updated encoder produces. By modifying only the image encoder, you avoid retraining the expensive language model and accidentally breaking the alignment it already has with human values.

The preference pairs come from unlabeled data: take any image, generate a clean version and an attacked version, let the model produce outputs for both, then treat the clean output as preferred and the attacked output as rejected. No human annotation required.

stages.s: Encoder now prefers clean images over attacked ones

math.words: The preference margin is the log probability of the correct response minus the log probability of the wrong response; training increases this gap by adjusting the image encoder parameters in the direction that widens it.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Start: encoder gives log p(correct on clean) = 2.1 (high confidence).
Start: encoder gives log p(confused on adv) = 2.0 (almost as confident in wrong).
After training, encoder gives log p(correct on clean) = 2.5 (stronger).
After training, encoder gives log p(confused on adv) = 1.2 (rejects it).
The encoder learned to widen the gap: from 0.1 to 1.3.

math.note: The margin grows because the encoder learns to extract visual features that the language model trusts on clean images and mistrusts on adversarial images.

charts.title: Traditional adversarial training

items.b: Preference pairs are only as good as the adversarial examples.
items.html: If your attack method is weak (does not actually fool the model), the encoder learns false preferences. Always use strong, diverse attacks.

items.b: Training only the encoder does not defend the language model.
items.html: If an adversarial image happens to produce features the language model already misinterprets, the encoder alone cannot fix it. The language model is frozen.
Training on a small model (TinyLLaVA) and transferring to a larger one (GPT-4o) works for efficiency, but some defense gains do not transfer perfectly. Large models have different failure modes.

items.b: Done right: use diverse attacks, include both clean and adversarial pairs, and measure both clean and adversarial accuracy to confirm no regression.
items.html: Validate on unseen datasets and attack types to ensure the learned preference generalizes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small vision-language model on a toy dataset (e.g., shapes or MNIST images). Train one version with standard adversarial fine-tuning and another with AdPO preference pairs. For both, measure accuracy on clean images, accuracy on attacked images, and the preference margin (confidence gap). Plot all three to show that AdPO maintains clean accuracy while boosting both attacked accuracy and margin, whereas adversarial training trades clean accuracy for defense.
demo.metric_eq: Preference margin = log p(correct output on clean) - log p(wrong output on attacked); Clean accuracy = fraction correct on unattacked images; Attacked accuracy = fraction correct on attacked images
demo.closing: The demo makes clear that preference optimization solves the conflict between defense against attacks and clean performance by treating them not as opposing forces but as two aspects of the same preference: always output the right thing.
